item.title: Finding solutions to cost of living. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is unfortunate to see recent figures which showcase that tax relief has resulted in no real reduction in the unusually high or fluctuating market prices -- a clear disservice to consumers who deserve some financial relief on basic goods.
The government reduced duties and taxes on 63 essential commodities in the FY27 budget, including rice, pulses, edible oil, spices, and agricultural products. Yet prices of many of these goods have remained high or even increased.
Reducing taxes and duties on essential goods is a welcome step when the cost of living continues to put pressure on ordinary families. However, this glaring gap between policy and reality remains a serious concern.
There are legitimate factors behind some of these increases: Traders have pointed to higher fuel costs, energy shortages, floods, heavy rainfall, and disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
While these pressures cannot simply be dismissed, they should not become a blanket explanation for every price increase either.
The onus is, therefore, on the government to strengthen market monitoring and determine where the benefits of tax concessions are going. If importers, wholesalers, or intermediaries are absorbing the savings instead of passing them on, consumers are effectively being denied the relief that public policy intended to provide.
This is particularly important at this point in time, when household budgets are already stretched; recent reporting has found families cutting back on food and household necessities as everyday expenses continue to rise.
Tax reductions should be accompanied by transparency, competition, and effective oversight. Relevant agencies need to regularly compare import costs, wholesale prices, and retail prices, and take action where unjustified margins or manipulation are found.
The objective of tax relief should ultimately be clear: Making essential goods more affordable.
The government has taken the first step, but now it must ensure that the benefit actually reaches the people it was meant to help.

item.title: Humanizing our prisons. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The crisis unfolding across the prison system in Chittagong is a stark reminder of a structural failure that can no longer be ignored.
Facilities designed to hold a combined capacity of 7,892 inmates are currently housing nearly 20,000 prisoners -- more than two and a half times what they were built to accommodate. At Chittagong Central Jail alone, 6,903 individuals are packed into a space meant for 2,249.
This severe deficit in physical capacity undermines the fundamental purpose of correctional institutions and violates basic human dignity.
When prisoners receive less than a fraction of the mandated living space, and when two or three inmates are routinely squeezed into berths meant for one, sanitation, health, and security rapidly deteriorate.
Worse still, space constraints prevent authorities from separating prisoners by legal status or the severity of their offenses. Placing petty offenders and pre-trial detainees alongside hardened convicts converts correctional spaces into breeding grounds for criminal networks rather than centres for rehabilitation.
Addressing this crisis requires immediate, multi-pronged intervention. While building additional facilities is a necessary long-term step, structural expansion alone will not solve the issue.
The judicial system must also expedite pre-trial proceedings and expand the use of bail for non-violent, minor offenses to relieve pressure on overcrowded cells.
Imprisonment was never meant to strip people of basic human decency. Treating inmates humanely is not a concession but an obligation, and is a reflection of civil society.
We expect the government to recognize the scale of the issue and take the necessary steps to allocate sufficient resources to expand prison capacity, modernize infrastructure, and enforce more humane living standards across all of our correctional facilities.

item.title: The real wall blocking the Bimstec free trade agreement. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Ask most analysts why the Bimstec FTA has gone nowhere since 2004, and you get one answer: Politics. Big powers can't agree, small states feel pushed around, and even after eight rounds of negotiation, the agreement remains far from finalizing their agreements.
But this article makes a sharper claim. Even if every Bimstec leader signed the agreement tomorrow, trade would barely move. The deeper problem isn't political will. It's the sheer unevenness of customs systems, product standards, and border infrastructure across the region. This is a regulatory problem, not a diplomatic one, and it needs a different fix.
The conventional account has real evidence behind it. The framework agreement was signed in 2004, but two decades later, its six parts, covering goods, services, investment, customs, trade facilitation, and dispute settlement, remain unfinished.
Bimstec's own Secretary-General has called the FTA's progress "very slow," and said member states are now considering finalizing only the parts closest to agreement instead of waiting for the whole package.
But this explanation has a problem. It can't explain why trade stays low even in product categories where tariffs are already fairly low, and even between countries with decent relations.
If politics were the whole story, trade should flow more easily where diplomacy is warmest. That isn't what happens. Something else is keeping goods stuck at the border.
It also can't explain why other regional blocs with their own share of political tension, such as Asean, still manage to trade far more with each other.
Look past the negotiating table and toward the customs shed, and the picture becomes clearer. The trade numbers are damning on their own.
Intra-Bimstec trade stood at 6.7% of members' total trade in 2023, translating into regional trade worth $53.49 billion, up from $46 billion in 2019. For a bloc that includes India, one of the world's largest economies, this is strikingly small.
The region's own data shows why. The Asian Development Bank's 2022 trade facilitation framework grades each country's customs systems against WTO standards. Thailand and India report 91.6% and 72.3% full compliance, with no procedures stuck in the weakest category. Myanmar, by contrast, has only 5.5% full compliance, with 85.3% still in the weakest category. Nepal fares similarly poorly, at just 2.1% full compliance.
This isn't a picture of political disagreement. It's a picture of infrastructure and staffing running at completely different speeds across the same trade bloc.
This unevenness costs real time and money at the border. A monitoring study of one Bangladesh trade corridor found that completing routine trade procedures took roughly half a month for an experienced trader, and 18 days for a new trader. Border crossing alone took over six hours for imports.
On a single 455-kilometre corridor, cargo trucks spent close to 30 hours in transit, over 11 of which were pure waiting time. These delays are not just an inconvenience for traders. They add directly to the final price of goods, which makes Bimstec-made products less competitive even inside their own region
And the type of barrier matters most. Sanitary and technical standards, rules on food safety, product testing, and certification, they all add up. These aren't simple paperwork checks. Smaller exporters struggle to meet them because compliance needs functioning testing labs, which many border regions simply don't have. When a country lacks a certified lab near its crossing point, an otherwise reasonable safety rule turns into an impassable barrier.
Put together, these threads tell a clear story. Bimstec's economies aren't only failing to agree on paper, they're also failing to converge in practice also.
Thailand's digitized customs system has almost nothing in common with Bhutan's land-port capacity. A signature cannot paper over that gap. It has to be built into the agreement itself, through shared testing facilities, mutual recognition of standards, and real technical assistance for the countries furthest behind.
Bimstec's own strategy documents admit this is still missing, noting that without mutual recognition agreements, exporters face costly duplicate testing every time a product crosses a new border.
This isn't just an argument over labels. It changes where Bimstec should spend its effort. If the problem were mainly political, the fix would be more summits and leader-level trust-building. But if the deeper problem is regulatory unevenness, summits are the wrong tool.
What's actually needed is slower, less visible technical work such as joint investment in border testing labs, mutual recognition agreements, harmonized paperwork, and dedicated funding for Myanmar, Nepal, and Bhutan, which remain decades behind on digitized border systems.
There's reason to think this shift is already happening inside the bloc. Officials have floated splitting the FTA into components and finalizing the parts closest to completion instead of waiting for the whole agreement at once. That is, in effect, an admission that the technical layer, not the political layer, is where real progress can happen fastest.
Bimstec's stalled FTA is usually told as a story about mistrust between governments. That story isn't false, but it's incomplete.
The data points to a different diagnosis: The region's real wall is regulatory, built from mismatched testing labs, uneven digitization, and standards nobody has agreed to recognize across borders.
Political summits will not fix this. Only steady, long-term work on fixing these rules and systems will. Until Bimstec makes that a top priority, its free trade agreement can’t boost trade alone.
Sachin Yadav, PhD scholar in International Studies, Jamia Hamdard University, New Delhi.

item.title: How can we tax?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We can say that some sorts of taxation are unfair. VAT, for example, weighs more heavily upon the poor than it does the rich.
We might therefore say that we should have more income tax and less VAT to make the system fairer: The rich will be carrying more of the tax burden that way.
Or perhaps we should tax profit, or companies, or dividends, or all the other things we could be doing.
This is the background to the report by Supro and Oxfam Bangladesh that the VAT system is regressive. Regressive in this sense means something specific. More of a poor person's income goes in this tax than the percentage of a rich person's. The report says 12.1% in a poor household compared to 5.9% in a rich one.
A progressive tax would reverse that, a progressive tax gets more of a rich income than it does of a poor one.
So, if we were to run the tax system purely on the grounds of fairness, then we'd change that system.
And that it should be the richer paying for society is an entirely fair idea. Even Adam Smith said that taxes should be “more than in proportion” to income -- the richer pay more of their income as a percentage than the poorer.
But there's something else here as well. That fairness is also called “equity,” and we do not only run the tax system on equity. We also have to include efficiency.
With taxation sometimes, this just means how easy it is to collect the money. How many bureaucrats we have to pay to get the cash. But there's another meaning as well and it's an important one.
Whatever we tax, we get less of. If we tax profits, then fewer people go into business to try to make profits. If we tax building houses, then fewer houses will be built. Tax incomes and some people will just not work so hard.
But how much less we get depends upon what the tax is. How much less business -- or houses, or work -- we get is called the “deadweight cost” of the tax. The things that just do not happen because we have decided to have this tax.
Yes, we do have to have tax. It's also true that the tax we raise can be used to do wonderful things. But it is still true that we get less of whatever we tax and so these deadweight costs exist.
We know the spectrum as well. It is land taxes, consumption, income, capital and profits, transactions. There are also sin taxes -- alcohol, tobacco and so on, but there, we're actually trying to make people do less, so that's not quite relevant.
No one is making more land so taxing it doesn't mean less of it. But as we start moving through consumption -- VAT is the obvious tax here -- to income taxes, corporate and capital gains taxes, then those deadweight costs rise. We lose more in economic activity that just does not happen for each same amount of tax revenue we collect.
Which gives us a problem. Yes, we can design a tax system which is fair and equitable. This would mean making the rich pay for everything out of their profits and high incomes.
But this tax system would be inefficient -- we'd be losing more business, more jobs, more development, if we tried to do it this way.
We could also just say darn to fairness and pay for everything from land taxes. There's actually a whole school of economics, Georgism, devoted to that very idea.
That also wouldn't raise very much which would mean we'd need a VAT as well which is the unfairness we noted up top.
The sad thing here is that there's no solution to this problem. No solution within economics that is. Whether you think we should be fair at the cost of inefficiency, or efficient but unfair, is something from morals, not economics.
You bring your ideas -- ideals -- of morals to economics but economics cannot tell you what the correct morals are.
Which leaves us with that little problem. Yes, we can make the tax system fairer. In doing so, we'll make it less efficient and make the future poorer.
So, just what is the right balance?
The only right answer is that this is a choice we have got to make.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Ensuring megaprojects deliver. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The Executive Committee of the National Economic Council’s (ECNEC) recent approval of the MRT Line-5 (Southern) and the cost revisions for MRT Line-1 and Line-5 (Northern) -- totaling an extraordinary Tk 2.5 lakh crore -- tells us that Bangladesh remains committed to expanding its urban infrastructure.
There is, of course, nothing wrong with this. Expanding mass transit is undoubtedly essential to relieve the capital city’s crushing congestion.
Yet, allocating capital on this unprecedented scale demands absolute financial accountability, meticulous execution, and a guarantee that every taka spent delivers direct, tangible improvements to daily life.
Mega-infrastructure projects in Bangladesh have historically suffered from a familiar set of systemic vulnerabilities: Frequent implementation delays, extensive cost overruns, and administrative bottlenecks.
When project budgets balloon, the public rightfully demands transparency into why original estimates fell short. External loans from foreign partners like Japan and the Asian Development Bank must be repaid by taxpayers; therefore, cost escalation, which has unfortunately become standard operating procedure, cannot remain the norm for how our nation functions.
Prudent financial management must go beyond initial approvals and funding arrangements. The relevant leadership and project authorities must implement rigorous oversight mechanisms, strict project timelines, and transparent auditing process from inception to delivery.
Ultimately, infrastructure is only as good as the benefit it brings to average citizens. A multi-billion-dollar metro network should not merely serve as a symbol of modernity -- it must translate into safer commutes, reduced traffic bottlenecks, improved air quality, and predictable travel times across the capital.
Large-scale public investment requires equally large-scale discipline. If we continue to fail in our management of these funds, and if inefficiency continues to be our status quo, the risk of unsustainable fiscal pressure will overshadow the very benefits these megaprojects are intended to bring.

How a Bangladeshi garment-maker is fighting the Middle East energy crunch. [ dawn ]
item.description:
A gas and power crisis has hit production at most Bangladeshi garment makers, but at 4A Yarn Dyeing, a supplier to Walmart, Gap and Next, workers stitch hoodies and attach brand logos uninterrupted, at least for now.

Since 2019, 4A has generated its own power, including through solar panels, making it an exception in Bangladesh’s garment industry, the world’s second-biggest exporter after China. The Middle East crisis has worsened energy shortages in the country where much of the electricity is generated using natural gas, furnace oil and diesel.

A recent survey of 134 knitwear factories found that 55 per cent had seen buyers cancel or cut orders because of gas and power shortages since late August, and 78pc had partially halted production. The factories also reported shipment delays and discounted orders to buyers.

But that’s not yet the case at 4A, whose factory on Dhaka’s outskirts employs nearly 7,500 workers and meets around 40pc of its electricity needs through solar, the rest mainly through its own gas and diesel generation.

“We never stayed at a single-source energy dependency. We had backups for everything,” said company co-owner Abdullah Hil Nakib.

“We need some sort of certainty. But the cost of doing business has increased. First there was a shortage of oil, then a shortage of gas.”

Costlier diesel has pushed 4A’s production costs up by 2 to 3pc, adding up to 5 million taka (Rs11.3m) to its monthly fuel bill, he said.

The pressure on factories intensified on Monday after Bangladesh raised fuel prices by up to 17.4pc, a move the government said was necessary because of soaring global prices and higher shipping costs due to the Middle East conflict triggered by US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February.

To reduce future disruptions, 4A plans to install an industrial-scale battery system that would allow operations to continue for several hours if power sources fail.

“We’ve been able to absorb the extra costs, but not every factory can afford to do that,” said Nakib, whose factory roofs are nearly covered in solar panels.

Steep fuel price hike to pile more pressure

Soaring gas import costs are slowing the country’s industrial growth, causing electricity outages and hurting spending on development projects due to higher gas subsidies, Bangladesh’s power minister said last week.

Bangladesh’s ready-made garment sector accounts for more than 80pc of export earnings, employs about 4m workers and contributes around 10pc to gross domestic product.

Some manufacturers have incurred additional costs by shipping goods by air or offering discounts to meet delivery deadlines after energy-related disruptions.

“Our margins are already very thin, and the fuel price hike will squeeze them further,” said garment exporter Shahidullah Azim.

“It is becoming increasingly difficult for us to absorb higher production and transportation costs while remaining competitive.”

Azim said a Canadian buyer that had been expected to order 25,000 pieces ultimately placed an order for only 8,000, which he attributed to declining buyer confidence amid Bangladesh’s economic and energy challenges.

Companies may be able to pay higher fuel costs, but gas shortages and power cuts are more worrying for some, given that those problems are not as intense in competitors like Vietnam and India, said Mohiuddin Rubel, additional managing director of Denim Expert Ltd, which supplies to brands including H&M.

“Whether we hold our position against other sourcing countries or lose ground to them depends on how well we manage it,” he said.

item.title: Rethinking waterlogging and flooding: Why our understanding matters. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On Sunday, 49mm of rain was recorded in Dhaka in nine hours that triggered widespread waterlogging in many parts of the city, causing disruptions to daily life and leaving commuters stranded.
Whenever there is flooding and waterlogging, we often see public frustration and criticism, indicating that this is a consequence of corruption, inadequate drainage networks, encroachment on wetlands and natural waterways, poor waste management, and unplanned urban expansion.
Many of these concerns are valid and should be reasonably addressed.
At the same time, we have to acknowledge that compared to the past, there have been improvements in infrastructural development -- and it is continuing.
Yet, why do we continue to face the same issues, sometimes even worse than before?
This is why our knowledge of climate change and its recent dynamics is also important to understand. Our widespread public perception is that economic development and improved infrastructure can eliminate these problems.
Investment in drainage systems, urban planning, and climate-resilient infrastructure is undoubtedly essential, but it is unrealistic to assume that development alone can completely shield cities from the forces of a rapidly changing climate.
Recent floods in some of the world's most developed cities indicate that even the best cities can be flooded and illustrate how rapid climate patterns are changing and challenging conventional planning assumptions.
On September 2, Toronto was hit by severe flooding after intense rainfall that overwhelmed drainage systems, disrupted transportation networks, and affected daily life.
On the same day, several cities in China's southeastern Fujian Province were inundated by torrential rains which were powerful enough to sweep away vehicles.
Similar flooding events have also been reported this year in New York City, Philadelphia, Washington DC, and Tokyo.
It shows that no city is immune to the growing risks of extreme weather. The fact that highly advanced and well-resourced cities continue to face devastating floods does not necessarily mean that their planning systems have failed.
Rather, it highlights a new reality: Many infrastructure systems designed using historical climate data have become obsolete.
Weather projections play a critical role in floodplain mapping and resilient infrastructure design. Yet at this time of history, climate projections are becoming increasingly difficult.
Hence, future development planning such as housing, roads, and bridges require a comprehensive understanding of climate change and its dynamics.
The recent Nepal disaster is a clear sign that climate related disasters can take shape in ways we never imagined possible. There is now this warning from the United Nations that natural climate phenomena such as El Niño may cause more extreme weather patterns such as droughts, flooding, extreme heat, and wildfires.
We are both a least developed country (LDC) and one of the world's most climate-vulnerable nations. Each year, millions of people are affected by climate-induced events, particularly during the four-to-five-month long monsoon season.
This year, the flooding in southern Chittagong, especially Banshkhali was a big shock to the local people who never imagined rainwater could trigger such a devastating flood situation in a coastal area.
If we only focus on governance and infrastructure failures, it will not be sufficient. Well-designed urban systems can and are overwhelmed by unprecedented volumes of rainfall and other climate-related shocks.
Thus, we should see flooding not only as an infrastructure challenge that can always be solved by engineering, but also as a rapidly changing climate challenge.
The assumption that every challenge can be permanently solved through human engineering or planning has created a false sense of stability for us.
In a world where environmental, social, and technological conditions are constantly changing, policies and long-term plans can become outdated more quickly than expected.
This is why climate education and awareness are an essential investment in our collective future. Climate education is not merely about acquiring knowledge, it is about preparing individuals, communities, and institutions to adapt to a world where environmental change is constant but uncertain.
Adaptation should not be viewed as a sign of weakness or failure. Rather, it is a practical and forward-looking strategy for navigating an uncertain future.
The goal is not to create systems that never fail, but to build societies that can learn, evolve, and respond effectively when conditions change.
Parvez Uddin Chowdhury is a development worker.

item.description:
Who gets to be Italian? The rise and rise of Islamophobia in Italy

Submitted by Dalia Ismail on Fri, 09/25/2026 - 13:30
Giorgia Meloni's announcement of a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools comes as the Italian right competes over the demonisation of Muslims
A Muslim takes part in a mass in Santa Maria in Trastevere church in Rome on 31 July 2016 (AFP)
Off

When Giorgia Meloni addressed hundreds of young supporters of her Brothers of Italy party in Rome on Sunday, she chose the school as a way of illustrating who she thought was and was not Italian. 

“It cannot be that, in an Italian classroom, Italian children are the ones who feel cornered because they have become the minority. It cannot happen,” the prime minister told Fenix, the annual festival organised by National Youth, Brothers of Italy’s youth wing. 

On Wednesday, Meloni’s government approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools and announced that a 30 percent cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school. 

Meloni described the measures as “common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate”.

The announcement comes as Italy moves towards an expected national election in 2027, with immigration, Islam and national identity once again central battlegrounds on the political right.

Meloni’s speech and the legislation immediately raised practical questions: who exactly is “foreign” and who is Italian? 

Italy already has guidelines recommending a 30 percent ceiling for pupils without Italian citizenship. The distinction between “Italian” and “foreign” children also rests on citizenship, rather than on where children were born or have grown up. 

Italy's citizenship system is based primarily on descent: children born in the country to non-Italian parents generally do not acquire Italian citizenship automatically. 

As a result, children who were born in Italy and have spent their lives there can still be officially classified as foreign citizens. And Meloni's intervention did not come in isolation.

A mosque in Mestre

Last week, a banner declaring “Your integration is our ruin” appeared outside a school in Mestre, on the mainland opposite Venice, in an area with a large Bangladeshi community. Nearby, at a public park used by Muslims for Friday prayers, “No Islam” and Christian crosses were painted on the ground and on a wooden structure.

The incidents come as a dispute over plans by members of Mestre's Bangladeshi community to build a permanent mosque and Islamic centre on the site of a former sawmill becomes increasingly heated. The community has bought the land, but the project requires approval from local authorities.

'We cannot allow an immigrant to become an Italian citizen so easily because then this citizen votes'

- Roberto Vannacci, Futuro Nazionale

One of the project's most vocal opponents has been Anna Maria Cisint, a European parliament member for the right-wing Lega party who has repeatedly campaigned against the construction of new mosques. 

In February, during a Lega protest outside the proposed site in Mestre, Cisint declared that the mosque would not be built if her political camp remained in power.

On the same Sunday that Meloni announced her school measures, Cisint appeared at the Lega’s annual rally in Pontida, the northern Italian town that has hosted the party's symbolic gathering for decades. 

She was joined on stage by four activists from Nemesis, a French far-right group that describes itself as feminist. The activists were wearing full-face veils. As people on stage and in the crowd chanted “take it off”, the women removed them.

“The threat is radical Islam,” Cisint told the rally. “We will never allow them to Islamise our home. Never.”

The convergence was striking. In Rome, Meloni warned that Italian children could become a minority in classrooms; at Pontida, a coalition politician warned of the country’s “Islamisation”; and in Mestre, a mosque dispute was enflamed by anti-Muslim slogans.

The rogue general

At the same time, another political force is trying to carve out space further to the right.

Roberto Vannacci, a former army general who first became a national figure after publishing a book attacking immigration, feminism and LGBTQ+ rights, entered the European Parliament in 2024 with the Lega. 

The “rogue general” later broke with the party and founded Futuro Nazionale, a new far-right movement that has made “remigration” - the removal of migrants from Italy - one of its defining themes. 

The party is now registering around eight percent in some opinion polls ahead of the next general election, while the Lega, still led by Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, has fallen below six percent. The figures have intensified a struggle over voters on the Italian right and over how far its politics on immigration and national identity can move.

It was against this backdrop that Vannacci made one of his most explicit statements yet about who should be allowed to become Italian. Speaking at a conference on urban security organised by a police union in Turin on 18 September, he argued that Italy should not make citizenship easier for immigrants.

“We cannot allow an immigrant to become an Italian citizen so easily because then this citizen votes,” Vannacci said. “And when he votes, he does not vote for the good of Italian citizens but for his own good.”

When challenged over whether he was simply worried that naturalised citizens would not vote for him, Vannacci replied: “I'm not afraid that they won't vote for me. I'm afraid that they won't vote for Italy.”

Who gets to be Italian?

The former general’s argument raises a fundamental question: what happens when the person born or raised in Italy actually becomes Italian. 

Fioralba Duma, an Italian-Albanian activist with the campaign group Italians Without Citizenship, told Middle East Eye that Meloni's remarks were particularly troubling because many of the children described as “foreign” have never known another country.

“It is sad, because you realise how little responsibility those in power take when dealing with such important issues, and how little they do to protect children and guarantee them equal opportunities,” she said.

'Petrol is approaching three euros a litre, and she is talking about girls wearing the niqab at school when there are no girls wearing the niqab at school'

- Ahmed Vall, Islamic Community of Rome

“Our struggle started 10 years ago - and for many people even earlier - but instead of reducing the number of people who are foreigners only on paper, that number continues to grow every year. We used to talk about newly arrived migrants. Today we are talking about third generations: the grandchildren of immigrants, born in Italy.”

Duma’s comments point to a contradiction that has become increasingly visible in Italy's political debate. 

Politicians can speak of “foreign pupils” in classrooms even when those pupils were born in Italy, have spent their lives in the Italian education system and may speak Italian as their first language.

Italy's citizenship law remains largely based on jus sanguinis, or citizenship by descent. A referendum in June 2025 sought to reduce from 10 to five years the period of legal residence required for non-EU adults to apply for citizenship. 

Around two-thirds of those who voted backed the proposal, but turnout was only around 30 percent, well below the 50 percent required for the result to be valid.

The Muslim threat narrative 

The controversy over the proposed mosque in Mestre shows how these arguments are playing out beyond the classroom.

Part of the city's large Bangladeshi community wants to turn the site of the former sawmill into a permanent Islamic centre capable of hosting up to 1,500 worshippers. But the project requires a change in the area's planning designation, and Venice's centre-right mayor, Simone Venturini, has opposed the project.

‘Our land is not for sale’: Italian activists challenge Israeli-linked solar projects
Read More »

Muslim organisations, meanwhile, accuse politicians of turning Islam into a political threat by focusing on issues that have little bearing on the everyday reality of Muslims in Italy.

Ahmed Vall, president of the Islamic Community of Rome, described Meloni's announcement on the niqab as “propaganda”. “We have never seen girls going to school wearing the niqab. It is a false problem,” he told MEE.

“Petrol is approaching three euros a litre, and she is talking about girls wearing the niqab at school when there are no girls wearing the niqab at school,” he said.

Vall said his organisation was prepared to challenge discriminatory measures through legal means, pointing to a complaint already filed against Lega MEP Silvia Sardone after she filmed and confronted a woman wearing a niqab in Turin. 

Rula Mohamed, another Islamic Community of Rome activist, described the situation more starkly, telling MEE that Islamophobia in Italy had reached “extreme levels”.

“What we are seeing today is the extreme result of something that has been cultivated for years,” she said. This climate, Mohamed argued, had been built not just by the right wing, but through years of Muslims being portrayed in the media as dangerous and incompatible with Italian society.

This, she said, had been compounded by the failure of much of the centre-left to seriously confront Islamophobia.

The case for digital banks. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank’s initial approval for five digital banks is an encouraging development for the country’s financial sector -- a move that can help accelerate the transition towards a more accessible, technology-driven banking system while creating new opportunities for people who remain underserved by conventional banking channels.
The proposed institutions, backed by businesses including bKash, Robi, Banglalink, and Square Group, will operate without conventional branches, providing banking services primarily through digital platforms.
This model could make financial services more convenient, particularly for people and small businesses that face difficulties accessing traditional banking facilities.
Bangladesh has already experienced rapid growth in mobile financial services, making the expansion of digital banking a natural next step.
There is also considerable potential for digital banks to support smaller borrowers and entrepreneurs: According to Bangladesh Bank, the new institutions are expected to focus on underserved customers and smaller loans rather than large-scale lending.
If managed responsibly, this could help broaden access to formal finance and support economic participation among people who have traditionally remained outside the banking system.
At the same time, innovation must be accompanied by strong safeguards. Digital banking will involve the collection and management of significant amounts of financial and personal data, making cybersecurity, consumer protection, and reliable digital infrastructure essential.
Bangladesh Bank must maintain rigorous oversight to ensure that technological convenience does not come at the expense of financial security or public confidence.
It is also important to remember that an initial approval is not a final license. The proposed banks must establish the necessary infrastructure and fulfil regulatory requirements before they can begin operations. This measured approach is welcome.
If the new banks combine innovation with accountability, security, and responsible lending, they could help make Bangladesh’s financial system more inclusive and efficient.
The move, therefore, represents a potentially important step towards a banking sector that better reflects the country’s increasingly digital economy.

item.title: Bangladesh’s 60-year energy test. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The Bay of Bengal is rarely calm. Off the coast of Cox’s Bazar, the water churns with a saline, metallic bite, where rusting hulls of floating storage units bob like corks on an endless expanse of gray.
You can smell the diesel, hear the hum of generators, and feel the oppressive weight of humidity when the grid fails. For a decade, this has been the harsh, transient reality of Bangladesh’s energy security -- a patchwork of floating FSRUs, rented by the year, vulnerable to the violent whims of cyclones.
But beneath the waves, an alternative has been proposed.
In early September 2026, Novatek Middle East presented Petrobangla with a $950 million offer for a gravity-based structure (GBS) LNG terminal. This is not a ship. This is a concrete leviathan, permanently welded to the seabed, engineered to withstand the most violent storms for 60 to 80 years.
It offers 7.5 MTPA capacity and claims to be 21% cheaper than a conventional land-based terminal. It is a beast built for an epoch, yet it sits on the desk of a government paralyzed by the politics of the present.
The GBS is a direct challenge to the status quo of energy insecurity. In international energy theory, this is the ultimate pursuit of energy security -- the physical protection of supply routes and resilient infrastructure.
FSRUs are fragile; they drift, they shut down, and they have historically knocked out hundreds of millions of cubic feet of capacity, plunging the nation into darkness. A GBS ends that cycle. It is an anchor of sovereignty in a turbulent ocean.
Yet, the silence from Dhaka is deafening. Why? Because while the leviathan waits in the water, a golden leash has already been attached to the state's neck.
Let us step back into the air-conditioned, leather-bound rooms of Washington, where the ink of a trade deal dried earlier this year. Under the banner of "Bangladesh First," the current regime signed an agreement that binds the nation to an estimated $15 billion in American energy products over 15 years, alongside a 0% tariff structure contingent on using US cotton.
This is not diplomacy; this is economic infrastructure designed to create institutional lock-in. Under neoliberal institutionalism, international agreements are designed to raise the cost of defection. We are now legally and commercially entangled in a 13-year Gunvor contract (117 cargoes at roughly $8.60/MMBtu), which bypassed open tenders and cemented a specific, expensive pricing structure into our grid.
The theory of trade dependency holds that nations bound by such agreements lose their strategic autonomy. To accept the Russian GBS, Dhaka would have to openly defy this Western pact. The price of defiance is a 19% tariff wall, diplomatic isolation, and the wrath of Washington.
The price of acceptance, however, is a structurally superior, cyclone-proof infrastructure that ensures national survival. This is the new " paternity suit " of international politics: The US deal claims ownership over our economic future.
But the true tragedy of this moment is not the geopolitical chessboard -- it is the ghost of our own neglect.
We have spent over $20 billion on LNG imports, yet less than $800 million on domestic exploration. In the classic language of the Resource Curse, we have abandoned our own endowment to fund our dependency.
We built a nation propped up by expensive, fleeting imports while our own gas fields remained trapped under the earth, waiting for state investment. The seabed GBS would finally provide a foundation, but it stands on the ruins of our own strategic failures.
This brings us to the unflinching crossroads. We have been told this government is built on "Bangladesh first." Is that a sincere doctrine, or is it a hollow slogan to be discarded when the tariff threats begin?
We must draw a line in the sand. The Bay of Bengal is not a theater for American or Russian proxy wars; it is the lifeline of a nation of 170 million people.
The GBS is not merely a Russian asset; it is an instrument of national resilience. The US trade deal is not just a commercial agreement; it is a cage that restricts our ability to make sovereign choices.
In international relations theory, we are witnessing a brutal clash between realism -- the survival of the state through physical power and durable defense -- and neoliberalism, where economic institutions dictate behaviour.
The current government is choosing the latter, trading physical resilience for bureaucratic comfort.
As the waves crash against the shores of Cox’s Bazar, indifferent to the politics of diplomats, the concrete leviathan remains a silent, waiting monument to what could have been.
The current government faces a historic test: Will they cut the golden leash, endure the short-term costs of trade disruption, and anchor Bangladesh to a century of energy sovereignty?
Or will they continue to float, rudderless, on the precarious tides of foreign dependency?
The decision defines whether "Bangladesh first" is an actual doctrine -- or just another diplomatic artifact destined for the dustbin.
Zakir Kibria is a Bangladeshi writer, policy analyst and entrepreneur based in Kathmandu, Nepal. He can be reached at zakir.kibria@gmail.com . The author previously explored these dynamics in " The Paternity Suit " for the Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Diesel at Tk 135: How will it affect your food bill?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In Bangladesh, whenever there is a hike in energy price, the consumers ask how much their food price is going to rise. The two are obviously related, but the amount that gets transferred from energy price to food price is not what it should be.
Diesel rose from Tk115 to Tk135 a litre on September 21, an increase of 17.4%. The recent price hike comes on the grounds that Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation’s loss has been mounting.
BPC lost Tk22,875 crore between March and August, and the budget FY 27 does not have any allocation to cover this loss. The Tk89,538 crore subsidy that the budget has provisioned for covers gas, electricity, and food.
BPC is recovering the loss by charging it to our pockets. But how much of the loss is it recovering? According to the government’s own formula, the market price for diesel should be Tk205 a litre. This means, at Tk135, we are still paying Tk70 less than what we should.
As such, the price hike only does a partial recovery of the loss for BPC -- about Tk10,000 crore of a Tk40,000 crore annual loss on diesel.
So was the price hike essential? Yes. Is it enough? No. Is there a risk of further price hike? Yes.
Then what would happen to the price of our food basket?
The evidence on how the rise in energy price transfers to food price in Bangladesh is scanty. Generally, the transfer is arbitrary and set by the traders.
We have results from April this year. The 15% adjustment then took food inflation from 8.39% in April to 9.06% in May, a gain of 0.67 percentage points in one month, before coming down to 7.02% by August. Non-food inflation rose and did not come back down.
In my reading, the current adjustment may add 0.7 to 1.2 percentage points to food inflation, with the peak in November or December.
However, that is the index. We need to measure what happens in the bazaars.
Let us look at one trader’s account from August 2022, after the largest rise in fuel price in our history. A Bogura trader moving fourteen tons to Dhaka increased his transport cost from Tk2 to Tk2.50 a kilogram. Freight is charged by weight, so that 50 poisha is what the lorry added to every kilogram of vegetable it carried, whatever the vegetable was.
In Dhaka, the price of okra went from Tk30 to Tk40 a kilo and long beans from Tk40 to Tk50. That 50 poisha of freight essentially translated to Tk10 a kilo for the consumer in Dhaka.
The Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection did the same arithmetic on eggs three weeks later and published it. Their estimate showed that the fuel price rise had added four poisha to the cost of moving one egg. Traders put Tk2.70 on the price, and the wholesale margin went from under 20 poisha to Tk2.70 in four days.
Historically, fish prices have not moved with the price of diesel. Dhaka's tilapia, pangash, and rui prices were the same in the week before the September hike and the week after, while the price of ilish fell.
Farmed fish depends on electricity rather than on diesel. In June 2023, with no change in fuel price, koi, pangash, and tilapia rose Tk40 to Tk50 a kilo when ice plants could not freeze blocks during load shedding.
Ilish fishermen are heavily reliant on diesel as they go out for days at a time. But it is a buyer’s market and they cannot transfer the higher cost of diesel to the price of their catch. The traders dictate.
How about rice? The price transfer is not immediate. The rice on sale in Dhaka today was grown with diesel bought between January and early April, when the official price was Tk100 but farmers were paying Tk110 to Tk125 through the March shortage.
The Tk135 announced on September 21 enters the Boro crop planted this winter and harvested in April and May 2027. The transport cost immediately increased for rice when the cost of diesel was hiked. Four days after the hike, a sack cost Tk15 to Tk20 more at wholesale, and Paijam and Atash went from Tk56 to Tk60 a kilo at Mohammadpur.
From the analysis, we can reach some conclusions:
• The hike was necessary and it is not finished. A further adjustment is the base case, not a risk.
• Vegetables, rice, fish, eggs -- each carries the fuel cost through a different channel and on a different timetable, so a single pass-through figure is meaningless.
• The gap persists because nobody analyzes how the value chain works, so the price shifts to whoever can charge the most without challenge.
How do we solve these challenges?
Ensure that people know that traders cannot just arbitrarily raise prices when energy prices are hiked, and the only way they will know is if someone publishes the number. As most people are unaware of how price is set and transferred across the levels of the value chain, they accept whatever comes their way. The default assumption here is that the price is bound to rise.
The government should set a threshold for how much margin can be added at each stage of the chain and this should vary by commodity. The price transmission should follow the variability. A threshold on the margin is not a cap on the price.
Publish what each stage of the food chain adds, every month, as a standing official series. Price caps do not work and have never worked. The Philippines capped rice in September 2023 and the national average came in 16% above the ceiling. Hungary capped retail food prices for 17 months and recorded the highest food inflation in the European Union.
What has worked is publication of the margin. South Africa's Competition Commission publishes an essential food price monitor that sets the producer price against the retail price commodity by commodity.
Hungary, having failed with caps, switched in 2025 to a ceiling on the retail margin published alongside a public price monitor.
A cap hides the mark-up. A published margin forces the chain to pass costs in both directions. Bangladesh already collects the daily prices through the Department of Agricultural Marketing. What it does not publish is the spread.
Economies are always correcting themselves. That is not the failure. The failure is when we cannot ensure the conditions that allow the economy to be resilient in stormy weather and bullish when the sun is shining.
In Bangladesh, our economic governance runs on perforated umbrellas. When it rains, we get wet. When the sun comes out, we burn.
Md Rubaiyath Sarwar is Managing Director, Innovision Consulting.

item.title: Rethinking public sector management and governance. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Effective public-sector management is fundamental to sustainable national development. Economic growth, social inclusion, environmental sustainability, and effective public service delivery ultimately depend upon the capacity of state institutions to formulate sound policies, manage public resources efficiently, enforce laws consistently, and maintain public trust.
Bangladesh has made substantial progress in economic and social development. However, sustaining and consolidating these achievements requires further strengthening of the institutional foundations of governance, including the rule of law, administrative accountability, civil service professionalism, merit-based human resource management, institutional integrity, and citizen-centred service delivery.
This series argues that weaknesses in public compliance should not be viewed solely as deficiencies in citizens’ civic consciousness. The effectiveness, consistency, and credibility of state institutions significantly influence citizens’ behaviour.
Where laws are consistently enforced and institutions operate predictably, citizens are more likely to comply. Conversely, selective or inconsistent enforcement can weaken public confidence and gradually normalise non-compliance.
My own experience in public administration over several decades has reinforced this observation.
In various capacities -- including assistant commissioner (land), magistrate, upazila nirbahi officer, deputy commissioner, senior official of different ministries, and managing director of a state-owned corporation -- I encountered situations in which professional and lawful decisions came into tension with the preferences of influential individuals.
On several occasions, I experienced pressure, threats, investigations, or transfers after declining to accommodate requests that, in my professional judgment, were inconsistent with applicable rules or the public interest.
These experiences strengthened my conviction that civil-service integrity cannot depend solely upon the personal courage of individual officers. It must be supported by institutional safeguards, transparent career-management systems, professional leadership, and accountability mechanisms that protect officials who act lawfully and in the public interest.
Bangladesh possesses a large pool of capable public servants recruited through competitive examinations. Yet recruitment alone is insufficient to create a high-performing public administration.
Continuous professional development, effective leadership, evidence-based career management, ethical standards, performance management, institutional incentives, and protection of professional integrity are equally important.
This series proposes the establishment of a human resources research cell (HRRC) within the Ministry of Public Administration. The proposed mechanism would undertake evidence-based research on civil-service workforce planning, competency development, career progression, leadership, organizational culture, performance management, integrity, and international best practices.
Ultimately, strengthening public-sector management is not simply an administrative reform agenda. It is an essential component of building state capacity, improving public service delivery, strengthening citizen trust, and achieving sustainable and inclusive national development.
Governance begins with the rule of law
“Country First” is a principle frequently invoked in public life. Its real significance, however, lies not in rhetoric but in whether public institutions and individuals consistently place the national and public interest above personal or sectional interests.
One of the most important manifestations of this principle is respect for the rule of law.
During official training abroad, I experienced a simple incident that provided an important lesson. On a holiday, three of us were returning to our destination after visiting a scenic location. We asked our vehicle driver to stop briefly beside a main road so that we could take a quick look around. He immediately declined.
When we asked why, he explained that parking on that section of the highway was prohibited by law. He regarded compliance not merely as a means of avoiding punishment but as an obligation to respect the laws of the state. He understood both the legal requirement and the consequences of non-compliance.
The incident raised an important governance question: Are citizens inherently unwilling to comply with laws, or does the effectiveness of public institutions shape citizens’ behaviour?
The experience suggested the latter.
A similar phenomenon can be observed in Bangladesh. In areas adjacent to cantonments, for example, drivers often demonstrate greater compliance with traffic regulations because enforcement is more visible and violations are more likely to result in immediate consequences.
As an assistant commissioner (land) at three different workplaces, I encountered several challenges in ensuring the lawful and transparent management of public resources. On one occasion, in an upazila, a superior authority sought to influence the disposal of trees that had fallen following a cyclone near a government office. There was pressure to dispose of the trees at a relatively low price.
I did not accommodate that pressure. Instead, I followed the prescribed procedure and arranged for the trees to be disposed of at a substantially higher value. The proceeds were deposited into the government treasury through the prescribed challan procedure.
Subsequently, an investigation was initiated against me following the intervention of the concerned authority. The investigation, however, found no wrongdoing on my part. On the contrary, the additional deputy commissioner (revenue) appreciated the manner in which I had performed my official responsibilities.
The experience reinforced a fundamental principle: An officer’s first responsibility is to the law and the public interest, rather than to the preferences of an individual superior.
This also illustrates a broader principle of governance. The credibility and consistency of state institutions influence public behaviour.
Accordingly, improving civic compliance requires more than awareness campaigns. It requires institutions capable of enforcing laws consistently, fairly, and predictably -- and public officials who can apply those laws without fear or favour.
State capacity and public-sector performance
Good governance depends upon state capacity -- the ability of public institutions to translate laws and policies into effective outcomes.
State capacity encompasses several interconnected dimensions:
A government may formulate sound policies, but their developmental impact will remain limited if implementing institutions lack adequate capacity.
My experience across field administration, the magistracy, ministries, development projects, and a state-owned corporation has demonstrated that institutional capacity depends not only upon formal structures but also upon the integrity and professionalism of the people operating those structures.
For this reason, public-sector reform should focus not only on creating new policies and institutions, but also on strengthening the organisational capabilities of existing institutions.
Political leadership and a professional civil service
In a democratic system, elected governments receive their mandate from citizens and establish political priorities. The civil service provides institutional continuity, technical expertise, policy advice, and implementation capacity.
These functions should be complementary.
A professional civil service should be responsive to the legitimate direction of the elected government while maintaining professional integrity, objectivity, and adherence to law.
Public servants are recruited through competitive examinations and are expected to develop specialized knowledge and professional competence throughout their careers. Their fundamental obligation should therefore be to the Constitution, the law, the state, and the citizens they serve -- not to individual political leaders or factions.
While serving in an upazila as assistant commissioner (land), I declined to implement what I regarded as an improper request from a divisional commissioner. Initially, I was threatened with adverse consequences, and subsequently, I was transferred to another workplace in circumstances that I perceived as punitive.
Similar experiences occurred at other stages of my career. While serving as a deputy commissioner, I declined to accommodate an irregular request from a state minister. Approximately a year later, I was transferred.
During my service in different ministries and while performing project-related responsibilities, I also encountered instances in which ministers, state ministers, and senior officials sought outcomes that, in my professional judgment, were inconsistent with established procedures.
These experiences did not lead me to conclude that political leadership and civil-service professionalism are inherently incompatible. Rather, they demonstrated the importance of establishing institutional boundaries within which political leadership can exercise legitimate democratic authority while professional officials can perform their statutory responsibilities without improper pressure.
The effectiveness of governance depends significantly on maintaining this appropriate relationship between democratic accountability and administrative professionalism.
Civil-service professionalism and institutional culture
During my career in public administration -- including field administration and service across different ministries and institutions -- I had opportunities through overseas training and professional engagements to observe administrative systems in other countries.
I found that effective public administrations generally place strong emphasis on professional dignity, transparency, competence, accountability, continuous learning, and public-service motivation.
Bangladesh also possesses a considerable pool of talented public servants. However, the effectiveness of a civil service cannot be determined solely by the quality of its recruitment process. The post-recruitment environment is equally important.
Formal training, in-service training, mentoring, leadership development, performance evaluation, ethical guidance, career planning, and organizational culture collectively determine whether individual talent is converted into institutional capability.
Where these systems are weak, public servants may experience excessive hierarchy, interpersonal or interdepartmental competition, inadequate intellectual development, limited transparency, risk aversion, and excessive dependence on informal networks.
These problems ultimately affect the performance of the state.
My own experience has shown that even an officer committed to professional integrity can become vulnerable when institutional safeguards are weak. Transfers, adverse administrative actions, or investigations can become instruments of pressure if personnel-management systems lack transparency and objective criteria.
Therefore, protecting civil-service professionalism requires more than exhorting individual officers to remain honest. The institutional environment must also make integrity professionally sustainable.
Meritocracy, integrity, and political neutrality
One of the most important principles of public-sector management is meritocracy.
Recruitment, promotion, posting, leadership selection, and professional development should be based primarily on competence, integrity, performance, and institutional need.
Political neutrality does not mean that the civil service should be unresponsive to an elected government. Rather, it means that public servants should implement lawful government decisions professionally without allowing partisan considerations to determine their professional conduct.
During my career, I served as a magistrate at different levels and participated in the adjudication of criminal cases. In performing judicial responsibilities, I sought to ensure that decisions were based on law and evidence, irrespective of external influence.
The experience reinforced my belief that public authority carries a corresponding responsibility. Whether an officer is exercising magisterial power, administering land, managing a district, implementing a development project, or managing a public corporation, the guiding principle should remain the same: Authority must be exercised in accordance with law and in the public interest.
Where political patronage becomes an important determinant of career progression, institutional incentives can become distorted. Officials may focus on cultivating relationships rather than improving professional competence and public-sector performance.
Such an environment can weaken institutional trust and undermine the long-term capacity of the state.
A professional civil servant should therefore not be measured by proximity to political power, display of authority, or accumulation of wealth. The appropriate measure is the quality, integrity, and public value of the service delivered.
Transparency and evidence-based career management
Transparency in public administration extends beyond financial disclosure or access to information. It should also encompass the processes through which public servants are evaluated, promoted, posted, disciplined, and assigned to strategic responsibilities.
Career decisions should be supported by objective evidence, including:
When an officer declines an improper request, there should be a clear distinction between legitimate administrative disagreement and punitive personnel action.
A transfer may sometimes be necessary for legitimate organisational reasons; however, personnel decisions should not become instruments for rewarding compliance with improper demands or punishing professional independence.
Institutional memory is particularly important during periods of administrative or political transition.
A professional public administration should avoid both rewarding officials merely because of political affiliation and penalizing competent officials because of perceived political association without objective evidence.
Personnel decisions should therefore be governed by transparent institutional processes rather than informal patronage.
This is essential for building a civil service that can maintain continuity and professionalism across successive governments.
Strategic human resource management
Modern public administration increasingly recognizes human resources as a strategic asset.
Governments invest substantially in infrastructure, technology, and physical institutions. Yet institutional performance ultimately depends upon the people operating those systems.
Strategic public-sector human-resource management should therefore address the complete employee lifecycle -- from recruitment to retirement.

Such an approach can help transform the civil service from a primarily personnel-administration system into a strategically managed professional workforce.
Professional integrity should also be treated as an organizational capability. An institution that recruits competent officers but does not protect them from improper pressure may ultimately lose the very capability it seeks to develop.
Establishing a human resources research cell

The HRRC could function as a specialised policy and research mechanism supporting long-term public-sector workforce reform.

Why true police reform remains Bangladesh’s unfinished revolution. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Viewing the Monsoon Revolution purely as a regime change, more than two years later, is a narrow, misconstrued perspective -- and a half-truth at best.
The popular uprising was never just about removing an increasingly authoritarian regime from power; its ambitions were far greater.
Rebuilding and reforming state institutions -- which had become inept, deeply corrupt and inefficient -- was the central underlying goal and subsequent focus of the 2024 July Revolution in Bangladesh.
What began as a student-led protest for merit-based public job quotas ultimately transformed into a sweeping national resistance against systemic corruption, authoritarianism, and the collapse of good governance and institutional accountability.
Once August 5 sealed the fate of the previous regime for the foreseeable future, an interim government finally held general elections, transferring power to the country's first elected government in nearly two decades.
This milestone ignited high aspirations that post-revolution Bangladesh’s dysfunctional, broken-down state institutions would finally be rebuilt to meet public expectations.
Unfortunately, that has not been the case.
The police force -- the backbone of the state’s law and order apparatus -- serves as a stark example. Over the past two years, spanning two successive administrations following the Awami League’s ouster, leadership across various tiers of the force has seen frequent shake-ups.
These changes have often appeared more politically-motivated than driven by professionalism. Furthermore, the period has been marked by a wave of forced and early retirements of high-ranking police officers.
For the broader population, these internal shuffles matter less than tangible results; the public simply desires a safer, more stable law and order situation, and a disciplined, professional police force that genuinely serves the people.
Unfortunately, recent developments -- such as lethal goons vandalizing public property late at night, sometimes within the immediate vicinity of police outposts -- clearly illustrate how rapidly public trust and institutional expectations are eroding.
Instead of a proactive police force, we are increasingly witnessing a reactive one, swinging into action and making sporadic arrests only after crimes have taken place in full public view.
The reason why a student-led protest demanding quota system reforms for government jobs so rapidly transformed into a nationwide uprising that culminated in a change of government was because the population harboured years of pent-up grievances over the collapse of state institutions, their persistent failure to deliver basic services, and unabated corruption.
While the quota system provided the initial spark and the regime change opened a window of opportunity, the underlying drivers of the movement were far more profound.
The July-August 2024 uprising, therefore, symbolized more than mere opposition to a specific system; it challenged the country’s entire development paradigm, which had long excluded the majority from its benefits while maintaining zero institutional accountability.
To re-establish this long-lost transparency, swift institutional reform should have been treated as the ultimate priority.
Unfortunately, much of the reform momentum gained during the Yunus-led transitional government has largely dissipated over the seven months following this year’s February elections.
Police reform is a stark example: the process has effectively stalled, slowing from high-stakes structural overhauls to cosmetic adjustments and deep institutional paralysis.
Following the July 2024 mass uprising -- where heavy-handed crackdowns resulted in the deaths of hundreds of protesters and sparked widespread public fury -- the interim government formed a dedicated Police Reform Commission in October 2024 to dismantle the force’s colonial-era command structure. However, the new parliament allowed the reform commission’s ordinance to lapse, creating a critical legislative vacuum.
Continuous changes of guard in the police hierarchy -- swapping leaders of one political inclination for another -- often offer a false promise of organizational revamp. Such superficial shuffling does little to instill genuine professionalism across the force.
When the public finds the police missing in times of emergency, replacing the faces of force commanders cannot restore eroded trust. Beyond superficial uniform alterations, forced retirements, and sweeping bureaucratic transfers, the force remains largely the shadow of its old self.
The new government, still in its first year in office, would render an invaluable service to the citizenry by completely dismantling this legacy of political weaponization.
The force must be brought under stringent public oversight and accountability. Only then can its members effectively serve the community, actively protecting citizens from everyday lawlessness, muggings, burglaries, and land grabs.
It is deeply troubling to see how a segment of grassroots politicians today stands accused of weaponizing young children and juveniles for so-called “gang” activities -- frequently under the very nose of law enforcement.
The tragic murder of a young boy, Apratim, in Comilla has laid bare critical allegations: That persistent police neglect in addressing prior offenses by these same perpetrators allowed local juvenile gangs to swell to such dangerous proportions.
Even more discouraging is the nature of the police response following Apratim’s death. The subsequent launch of sweeping, overnight drives has led to the wholesale detention of hundreds of young people. While such knee-jerk, high-handed sweeps might temporarily succeed in shifting the spotlight away from institutional negligence, they do nothing to mend a broken law and order ecosystem.
Criminalizing our youth en masse fails to address the root problem; it denies juveniles the healthy, supportive socio-political environment they desperately need to thrive away from a life of crime.
Wholesale drives and indiscriminate detentions of adolescents universally fail to contain juvenile gang activity over the long term. While mass sweeps provide a temporary visual deterrence that may briefly appease public anxiety following high-profile crimes, they act as little more than a bandage on a deeply systemic issue.
Because mass arrests frequently rely on physical appearance, location, or arbitrary gathering spots rather than specific evidence, they end up sweeping innocent adolescents alongside hardened ringleaders. This approach fosters deep resentment towards law enforcement and severely traumatizes minors who have committed no crimes.
Furthermore, when these youths are sent to overcrowded child development centres or regular judicial custody, they receive virtually no meaningful rehabilitation. Criminological studies consistently indicate that arrested juveniles frequently return to their neighbourhoods only to regroup, recruit new members, and change their gang names -- often becoming far more hardened by their time inside.
Crucially, juvenile gangs (locally known as kishor gangs ) do not operate in a vacuum. Instead, they are actively patronized by local political leaders and their criminal associates, who deploy these youths for territorial control, extortion, and political muscle.
Mass drives merely target expendable, underage foot soldiers while leaving the older, influential puppet masters entirely untouched.
Until the police force is fundamentally reformed, systemic corruption and inefficiencies will continue to lure officers into ignoring routine community policing and gang tracking, incentivizing them instead to conduct flashy mass detentions of minors while leaving politically linked adult handler networks unscathed.
The current BNP leadership and the government they administer must remain mindful of the harsh lessons a preceding BNP administration learned at a heavy cost in the early 2000s. Following the BNP’s assumption of office in late 2001, Bangladesh experienced a severe spike in violent crime, including rampant extortion, high-profile kidnappings, muggings, vigilante justice, and murders.
The response that followed -- a massive, joint military campaign known as “Operation Clean Heart” -- resulted in widespread human rights controversies that no modern, democratically-elected government should ever seek to emulate.
A reformed police force -- shielded from undue political influence and empowered to deliver public law and order professionally -- is the only sustainable deterrent against resorting to such heavy-handed military measures to tackle societal crime.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Revenue generation needs long-term planning. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The International Monetary Fund’s critical assessment of the National Board of Revenue’s (NBR) latest reform roadmap exposes a fundamental truth that has been an issue for Bangladesh for years: Short term, superficial administrative adjustments cannot resolve our chronic fiscal woes.
Despite repeated pledges to modernize tax collection and broaden the revenue base, it is disappointing that the NBR remains crippled by structural loopholes, slow execution, and a reliance on ad-hoc targets.
For a country maintaining one of the lowest tax-to-GDP ratios in South Asia , hovering under 8%, we must stop treating tax reform as a bureaucratic compliance exercise rather than the national priority it is.
The IMF’s critique rightly targets the core flaws of our revenue architecture. Rather than pursuing systemic modernization through comprehensive digitization, structural decoupling of tax policy from enforcement, and the elimination of discretionary exemptions, the revenue authority routinely defaults to squeezing existing taxpayers.
Setting ambitious revenue targets without fixing systemic leakages or curbing widespread tax evasion yields predictable shortfalls year after year. Furthermore, the persistent delay in fully automating tax administration and streamlining VAT collection perpetuates an environment ripe for rent-seeking and corruption.
Bangladesh can no longer afford an inefficient revenue apparatus. With growing debt-servicing obligations, rising social spending needs, and critical infrastructure demands, sustainable fiscal health depends on a modern, equitable, and transparent tax system.
As such, we hope and expect those at NBR to recognize that we learn to plan for the long term. For that to happen, we must start focusing on high-income earners and corporate entities currently operating outside official channels, rather than overburdening compliant businesses and middle-class citizens through indirect taxation.
Real reform requires genuine political will, not administrative posturing to satisfy multilateral lenders. Until the government replaces half-hearted measures with deep, structural reform, our fiscal stability will remain shaky.

item.description:
Bangladesh’s export performance in the first quarter of FY27 offers a welcome sign of resilience, especially at a time when the economy continues to face a range of challenges.
According to reports, merchandise exports rose by 6.34% year-on-year to $13.09 billion between July and September, while September alone recorded an 8.54% growth.
The continued strength of the readymade garment sector is also particularly encouraging. RMG exports grew 6.10% during the quarter to $10.58b, with both knitwear and woven garments recording solid growth.
This remains an important source of foreign exchange and employment, and its performance demonstrates the continued competitiveness of Bangladeshi exporters in global markets.
More encouraging still is the performance of several non-RMG sectors. Pharmaceutical exports grew 40.39%, while jute and jute goods rose 31.55%, leather and leather products 14.74%, and light engineering 16.51%.
These figures are proof that Bangladesh has considerable potential beyond its traditional dependence on garments.
However, this progress should be treated as an opportunity to build on rather than a reason for complacency. Agricultural products and frozen and live fish recorded negative growth, showing that important areas of the export basket still require attention.
Greater diversification will be essential if Bangladesh is to make its export earnings more resilient to changes in global demand.
The government must therefore focus on removing the structural obstacles that continue to affect exporters, including energy shortages, high production costs, logistical bottlenecks, and bureaucratic delays.
Support for product upgrading, market expansion, and trade facilitation must translate into practical measures that businesses can actually benefit from.
The latest figures are undoubtedly positive: They reflect the efforts of exporters and workers and the continued demand for Bangladeshi products.
Now, the priority should be to sustain this momentum, strengthen emerging sectors, and open more markets so that export growth becomes broader, more stable, and capable of supporting Bangladesh’s long-term economic ambitions.
